summary: Describes a model for setting up IP addresses and subnet prefixes on the interfaces of routers that connect to links whose connectivity is not well defined, as in ad hoc wireless networks. It is informational and not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: In a game where players keep moving around, you cannot assume who is next to whom. This explains how to give out network addresses when neighbors keep changing.

subtitle: How to configure router interface addresses and prefixes when you cannot know who is on the other end of the link.

tldr.problem: On ad hoc networks, link connectivity is unplanned or changes over time, so there is no standard way to decide how to configure IP addresses and subnet prefixes on router interfaces.
tldr.mechanism: The model says to configure no on-link subnet prefix on such an interface (a 32-bit prefix for IPv4) and to make each address unique at least within the routing domain.
tldr.outcome: This is guidance in an Informational document, not a standard. It lets routing protocols and forwarding function without promising neighbors that are not guaranteed.

facts.label: Address uniqueness
facts.value: At least within the routing domain

sections.title: The Problem with Undetermined Links
sections.content:
Correct IP addresses and subnet masks on router interfaces are generally a prerequisite for routing protocols to work. When links are well known and stable, the design is straightforward. When connectivity is undetermined, meaning unplanned or time-varying, there is no canonical method. Ad hoc networks are the typical example.

The document gives a model for configuring addresses and prefixes on router interfaces to such links so that routing protocols and data forwarding can function. It deliberately covers only the configuration needed for routing and forwarding. Prefixes for applications on the routers or for attached hosts are treated as a separable problem.
sections.plainLanguage: When nobody knows who will be your neighbor from minute to minute, you need simple rules for choosing an address that still work.

sections.title: The Two Principles
sections.content:
The first principle covers subnet prefixes. If a link allows no assumptions about connectivity to other interfaces, the only addresses that can be assumed on-link are the interface's own. So no on-link subnet prefix should be configured on such an interface. If layer 2 communication exists between two interfaces, IP packets can still be exchanged even without matching subnet configuration. If assumptions about connectivity or persistent reachability can be made, they should be considered and an on-link prefix may be used.

The second principle covers addresses. Routing protocols differ in how unique addresses must be: some have no requirement, others need local uniqueness, others need uniqueness within the routing domain. Those with no requirement use a separate identifier inside the protocol. An address unique at least within the routing domain satisfies all of them, so an address on such an interface should be unique, at least within the routing domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not tell the network that a whole street is right next to you when you cannot be sure. And give yourself a name no one else in the neighborhood has.

sections.title: IPv6 and IPv4 Models
sections.content:
For IPv6, the rules are: the address should be unique at least within the routing domain, and no on-link subnet prefix is configured on the interface. IPv6 makes this clean because it allows leaving the on-link prefix out entirely.

For IPv4, the address should likewise be unique at least within the routing domain, and any subnet prefix configured on the interface should be 32 bits long.

Link-local addresses are of limited use here. There is generally no mechanism to ensure IPv6 link-local addresses are unique across multiple links, though those built from a modified EUI-64 identifier should be globally unique. Routers also cannot forward packets with link-local source or destination addresses to other links, and routers mostly need to forward between links. So autoconfiguration should primarily focus on addresses that are not link-local. IPv4 link-local addresses (RFC 3927) should be discouraged for most applications for the same reasons, made worse by the smaller pool and greater reliance on Duplicate Address Detection.
sections.plainLanguage: For the newer address style, just leave out the neighborhood size. For the older style, say you are a neighborhood of exactly one house. Skip the addresses that only work on one street.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The model is not said to introduce new security threats. The generic routing threats in RFC 4593 still apply. However, the possible lack of pre-established infrastructure or authority on such links may make some of those attacks easier, and malevolent misconfiguration may be harder to detect and locate.
sections.plainLanguage: With no central office handing out addresses, it is easier for someone to cheat and harder to catch them.
